facts.claim: Julian Orr's fieldwork examined U.S. Xerox copier technicians and found oral stories central to diagnosis and knowledge circulation.
facts.mechanism: Because technicians narrated symptoms, attempted fixes, and machine behavior to peers, experience became a socially distributed diagnostic resource.
facts.commonError: Orr found that technicians worked only from manuals and avoided peer conversation.
facts.whyWrong: His ethnography emphasizes talk and circulating stories as instrumental parts of successful repair practice.

facts.claim: Pham and Taylor assigned college freshmen to mental-simulation conditions for 5 to 7 days before a midterm examination.
facts.mechanism: Because repeated rehearsal occurred while real preparation choices were still available, the simulation could influence planning and study behavior.
facts.commonError: Participants imagined an exam only once after they had already completed it.
facts.whyWrong: The intervention ran prospectively across the preparation period before the test.

facts.claim: In Pham and Taylor's study, process simulation enhanced studying and exam grades through improved planning and reduced anxiety.
facts.mechanism: Because rehearsing concrete study steps exposed when and how to act, participants formed better plans and reduced uncertainty around performance.
facts.commonError: Imagining the pleasure of the final grade produced the same planning mechanism as rehearsing study steps.
facts.whyWrong: Outcome imagery represents success, whereas process imagery rehearses the behaviors that can produce it.

facts.claim: A 1999 Indiana Daily Student story brought attention to Jared Fogle's reported 245-pound weight loss before Subway's 2000 national campaign.
facts.mechanism: Because the discovered account contained a recognizable before-and-after challenge arc, advertisers could build a narrative around transformation rather than a list of low-fat menu items.
facts.commonError: Subway invented the entire weight-loss story first and then commissioned a fictional student newspaper article.
facts.whyWrong: The campus story preceded the national advertising campaign and helped the case reach the company.

facts.claim: The historical Jared Fogle campaign cannot safely function as present-day moral endorsement because Fogle was later convicted of crimes involving minors.
facts.mechanism: Because later verified conduct radically changes the ethical associations of the spokesperson, retelling the campaign as uncomplicated inspiration would mislead current readers.
facts.commonError: Source fidelity requires ignoring all later public facts about a real figure used as an inspirational model.
facts.whyWrong: Historical accuracy includes material context needed to avoid turning a communication example into praise of the person.

facts.claim: Stephen Denning's World Bank springboard case centers on a June 1995 health worker in Kamana, Zambia, finding malaria information online.
facts.mechanism: Because one small successful knowledge-sharing episode made a possible future visible, listeners could imagine scaling the pattern across the institution.
facts.commonError: The springboard method requires a long heroic biography with every technical implementation detail.
facts.whyWrong: Its function is to trigger the audience's own future story, so a concise true instance can be more generative than exhaustive narration.

facts.claim: The three inspirational plot families are Challenge, Connection, and Creativity.
facts.mechanism: Because they model overcoming obstacles, bridging social distance, or solving a problem resourcefully, each plot supplies a different route to motivated action.
facts.commonError: All inspirational stories must use a lone hero defeating a physical opponent.
facts.whyWrong: Connection and Creativity plots can inspire through relationship or ingenuity without a conventional contest.

facts.claim: A process story functions as mental simulation when it preserves goals, obstacles, choices, actions, and consequences.
facts.mechanism: Because listeners can map the sequence onto a future situation, the narrative rehearses responses before real stakes arrive.
facts.commonError: A story teaches action best when all decisions and causal links are removed in favor of a one-line moral.
facts.whyWrong: Removing the sequence discards the cues that show when and how the lesson applies.

facts.claim: A springboard story describes a real successful instance that helps listeners imagine analogous change in their own environment.
facts.mechanism: Because the case proves that a nearby possibility has already occurred, the audience can construct its own forward-looking scenario with lower disbelief.
facts.commonError: A springboard story is valuable only when listeners copy every surface detail exactly.
facts.whyWrong: The audience transfers the underlying possibility and mechanism, adapting details to its own context.
